notes:
I've put together notes for every verse, but some are thinner than others. A few things to know first:

- **Coverage:** Enduring Word's page cut off at v. 10, so I couldn't use David Guzik for vv. 11–18.
- **Not covered:** I didn't get to the netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes, Orthodox sources (oca.org), Lutheran sources other than one 1517.org article, Anglican sources, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those are left out rather than guessed.
- **Catholic view:** this comes from the Haydock Catholic commentary (an older Catholic Bible commentary) on biblehub.com, not from newadvent.org or catholic.com.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - "Therefore" turns the point of chapter 1 (Jesus is greater than the angels) into something to act on. Guzik notes the letter was written to Christians, not unbelievers. Heeding means both hearing carefully and doing what you hear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - The picture is a boat with no anchor drifting with the current. The Greek word means "to slip," and was used of an arrow slipping from a quiver. Guzik's point is that leaving the faith is usually slow drifting, not a sudden break. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - Ellicott says the Greek verb means flowing or floating past something. The danger is missing the gospel through carelessness. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/2-1.htm
  - Wesley pictures the truth slipping away "as water out of a leaky vessel." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock uses a similar picture: water running out of leaking vessels and lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**vv. 1–3 (where traditions differ: who is being warned, and can a believer fall away?)**
- **MacArthur (Baptist):** the warning "cannot be to Christians," who already have salvation. He reads it as aimed at Jews who were convinced in their heads but never committed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_23
- **J. Vernon McGee:** the verse has nothing to do with whether a believer can lose salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_23
- **Other writers on Precept Austin:** some argue the thing at stake in all five warning passages is loss of salvation, not loss of rewards. Others say the warnings are a means God uses to keep the elect in the faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_21-3
- **Steven Cole (bible.org):** true believers may drift, but when confronted they turn back. Those who don't turn back have no basis for assurance. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-4-danger-drifting-spiritually-hebrews-21-4
- **Bob Utley (bible.org):** lists three possible audiences: people who never responded, believers who hadn't matured, and believers at risk of not holding on to their confession. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21438
- **Sinclair Ferguson (Ligonier, Reformed):** apostasy really happens, and the drifting of 2:1 is often slow and unnoticed. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/apostasy-and-how-it-happens
- **Gospel Coalition (Canada):** Hebrews makes clear that not everyone who professes faith will last to the end. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/straight-paths/danger-falling-away/
- I couldn't find a Wesleyan, Pentecostal or Lutheran source on this question specifically.

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - "The message spoken by angels" is the Law of Moses, which angels helped deliver (Deut 33:2; Acts 7:53; Gal 3:19). It was strict and had to be taken seriously. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - Wesley: God spoke the law through angels but the gospel through his Son. "Transgression" means doing wrong; "disobedience" means leaving duty undone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
  - Utley notes the two Greek words share a prefix and may be a deliberate wordplay. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21438

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The argument runs from lesser to greater: a greater message from a greater Person brings greater condemnation if it is ignored. The Greek word for "neglect" is the one used in Matthew 22:5 of guests who brushed off a wedding invitation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - "Confirmed to us by those who heard Him" shows the writer was not an eyewitness. Guzik gives this as one reason some doubt Paul wrote Hebrews. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - Wesley: the salvation is "great" because it rescues from great wickedness and misery into great holiness and happiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 4 (where traditions differ: have the miraculous gifts ceased?)**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott: God bore witness alongside the preachers to the truth they preached. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/2-4.htm
  - Wesley: the signs and wonders came during Jesus' life, and the miraculous gifts were handed out after his exaltation, by God's will, not the will of those who received them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- **Cessationist (Baptist):**
  - MacArthur (gty.org) says these gifts were "the signs of an apostle." He holds that the gift of miracles ended with the apostolic age, though he says he isn't claiming miracles themselves have stopped. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1214/miracles-healings-and-tongues?Term=gift+of+healing
  - Precept Austin quotes MacArthur that God now bears witness through his written Word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_24
  - Biblehub's article on cessationism uses vv. 3–4 to argue the signs authenticated the apostles while the church was in its infancy. https://biblehub.com/q/what_is_cessationism.htm
- **Continuationist (charismatic):**
  - Sam Storms says the word "apostle" doesn't appear in the passage, and "those who heard" need not mean only the apostles. He adds that the writer separates "miracles" from "gifts," and nobody restricts teaching or mercy to the first century. He finds nothing here that requires the cessationist view. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/hebrews-2-and-the-continuationist---cessationist-debate
  - A bible.org article argues the present-tense participle may mean God kept on confirming the message, and points to Hebrews 6:4–5 as evidence the gifts continued. https://bible.org/article/questions-cessationists-should-ask-biblical-examination-cessationism
- **Middle view (Guzik, Enduring Word):** if there is nothing miraculous at all, true belief may be in question. But miracles can't be "worked up" by enthusiasm. He treats denying the gifts and faking them as equally dangerous. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
- **Catholic:** Haydock says miracles became less frequent as they were less needed, but denies they were ever fully withdrawn. He claims every age since the apostles has seen miracles in the Catholic Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - God never gave angels the kind of rule over the world that he gave humanity (Gen 1:26–30). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - Wesley takes "the world to come" to mean the age of the Messiah, the era that followed the Mosaic one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock reads it as the Church of Christ, subject to Christ, whereas the old law came through angels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**vv. 6–8**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Psalm 8 shows how small humans are next to God, and also the rule God gave them. Here the writer turns from Jesus' deity (ch. 1) to his full humanity. Guzik warns against Docetism, an early false teaching that Jesus only seemed human. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - Wesley: the psalm applied in some sense to Adam, but in its fullest sense only to "the second Adam" (Christ). He notes the Hebrew reads "a little lower than God," and the apostles quoted the Greek Septuagint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
  - On "not yet": Wesley says this rule is plainly not yet true of humanity in general. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock applies the psalm especially to Christ's human nature. He says everything will be fully subject to Christ only at the end of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 9 (where traditions differ: for whom did Christ die?)**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott: Jesus is the one in whom the psalm is completely fulfilled, and his exaltation makes possible the exaltation of "the many." He links the honor to Jesus' obedience to death and reads "taste death" as tasting all its bitterness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/2-9.htm
  - Textual note: Ellicott reports that many manuscripts known to the church father Origen read "apart from God" instead of "by the grace of God." He judges that reading "almost certainly incorrect." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/2-9.htm
- **Reformed:**
  - Gill says Christ became man "that he might die for his church and people." He mentions a possible rendering, "taste of every death," which would remove the argument for a universal atonement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/2-9.htm
  - Erik Raymond (TGC) says "everyone limits the atonement": Arminians limit its power, Calvinists limit its extent. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/erik-raymond/jesus-die-everyone/
- **Wesleyan and others:**
  - Wesley: "every man," meaning everyone who ever was or will be born. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
  - Barnes, a Presbyterian of the "New School" (a camp that held to general atonement), asks how words "could affirm more clearly" that the atonement was unlimited. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/2-9.htm
  - Clarke, a Methodist, says Christ died in place of every human soul. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/hebrews/2-9.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock says Christ died for all, "not only for the predestinate or the elect." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 10**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - It was "fitting" for God to save at the cost of the Son's suffering, because real love costs something. Jesus is the "captain," the leader who goes ahead of his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-2/
  - Wesley: it suited God's justice, goodness and wisdom. "Perfect" means Christ was made a complete sin-offering. Wesley stresses he was already perfect before he suffered, and this verse is not about us being saved by our own sufferings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock says this was not absolutely necessary but a fitting way to show God's goodness and justice. Christ was made a perfect sacrifice for the sins of all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 11**
- Wesley: "of the same family" means sharing one nature, from one parent, Adam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) agrees: the same human nature, descended from Adam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 12**
- Wesley: Christ is like the leader of the choir. He did this literally among his apostles the night before he died (Psalm 22:22), and still does it through his word and Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 13**
- Wesley: "I will put my trust in Him" shows Christ sharing his brothers' sufferings. "The children" are believers, presented to God as younger brothers (Isaiah 8:17–18). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 14**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Pulpit Commentary: "destroy" means to bring to nothing or make powerless. Satan was allowed dominion over death because of human sin. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/2-14.htm
  - Wesley: Christ broke the devil's tyranny, a power the devil held only by God's permission. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
  - Spurgeon: Christ did this "not by his example, not even by his life, but by his death." https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_214-15
- **How the cross defeats the devil:**
  - John Piper (Desiring God, Baptist) compares v. 14 with v. 17. He concludes that Christ makes the devil powerless by atoning for our sins, which takes away the devil's only deadly weapon. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jesus-is-able-to-help-those-who-are-tempted
  - Ligonier quotes Calvin: the devil still lives, but his power to hurt us is destroyed or restrained. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/deliverance-from-death
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** angels serve us, but Jesus becomes one of us. "The incarnation of God in Christ is pure gospel." https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-hebrews-21-13-14-18-pentecost-19-series-b
- **Catholic:** Haydock says the devil ruled through death by tempting people to sin. Christ, "the life and source of life," beat both the devil and death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott thinks the verse comes from the writer's sympathy with persecuted Christians who were being pressured to abandon the faith. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/2-15.htm
- Wesley: anyone who fears death lives in bondage, and everyone who doesn't know Christ fears it to some degree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- Spurgeon: Christ removes the fear by removing sin, death's sting, and by changing death from an execution into a deliverance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_214-15

**v. 16**
- Wesley: Christ took on human nature, not angelic nature. "Abraham" is named because the promise was made to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- Haydock (Catholic): Christ never united angelic nature to himself to save fallen angels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 17**
- Wesley: "merciful toward sinners; faithful toward God." The verse sums up what came before and introduces the high-priest theme of later chapters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
- Gill: Christ couldn't be a high priest unless he was human, and couldn't be merciful unless he shared our sufferings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/2-17.html
- Haydock (Catholic): like us in all things, "sin always excepted." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/hebrews/2.htm

**v. 18 (where interpreters differ: could Jesus have sinned?)**
- Ligonier (Reformed) says Christ never sinned, "nor could He." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/helping-tempted
- Precept Austin sets out the debate:
  - Henry Morris: Jesus could not actually have sinned, because he is God.
  - Wayne Grudem: it was not possible for him to sin, yet the temptations were real, because he didn't lean on his divine nature to resist them.
  - Geisler: notes that other orthodox scholars think sin was possible but never actual. Denying that, they argue, would turn his temptation into a charade.

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_218
- Coffman (Churches of Christ) argues no one can be tempted to do what they cannot do. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/2-17.html
- Wesley: Christ has given clear proof that he can help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/2.htm
